aboutAuthor: Howard Marks is co-founder and co-chairman of Oaktree Capital Management, renowned for his client memos on risk and cycles. His writing distills decades of distressed debt experience into temperate, practical wisdom for navigating markets.

points.heading: Position, don't predict
points.body: Cycles cannot be timed to the month, but your position on the pendulum between fear and greed can be judged. Returns come from calibrated offense when compensated and disciplined defense when not, regardless of forecast.

points.heading: Psychology drives price more than fundamentals
points.body: Earnings oscillate modestly while multiples swing violently. The pendulum illustration of euphoria versus despair shows belief driving buying that validates belief until price divorces from value.

points.heading: Credit is the oxygen of cycles
points.body: Easy credit lifts collateral that justifies more credit; tight credit forces selling that creates bargains. Windows that look open widest when spreads are thinnest are precisely when risk is highest.

points.heading: Mean reversion is gravity
points.body: Peak margins, peak multiples, and record issuance all invite reversal via competition and cost. Fan charts of margins reverting warn that today's peak should be doubted, not capitalized.

points.heading: Structure limits matter more than insight
points.body: Benchmarks, redemption rights, and career risk force procyclical behavior even when you know better. The distressed cycle rewards those who built mandates and reserves during euphoria.

points.heading: Success cycles too
points.body: A hot hand after three great years breeds asset growth, style drift, and hubris. The lifecycle map from struggle to complacency reminds that winning must be managed as vigilantly as losing.

insights: The pendulum between greed and fear, not GDP, is the most reliable indicator of where you are in the market cycle.
The credit window opens widest when compensation is thinnest, planting the next forced-selling opportunity.
Being early and being wrong are indistinguishable without staying power, so reserves and humility are the true edge.
conclusion: Mastering the Market Cycle turns a lifetime of Oaktree memos into a portable discipline: know history, read behavior, respect credit, and keep dry powder so that when pendulums swing, you can lean the other way without being forced to flinch.
